title: What are the two common CountDownLatch patterns (startup gate and completion gate), and why can a latch not be reset — what do you use instead?

s1_definition.profdef: `CountDownLatch` is a one-shot synchronization aid initialized with a count. Threads call `await()` to block until the count reaches zero, and other threads call `countDown()` to decrement it. Once it hits zero it stays zero forever — there is no reset. Two canonical patterns exist: a startup gate (count 1) where many worker threads wait on a single latch so they all begin at the same instant, and a completion gate (count N) where a coordinator waits for N workers to each count down as they finish. Because a latch cannot be reused, for repeated phases you use `CyclicBarrier` or `Phaser`.
s1_definition.analogy: The startup gate is like a bank branch where ten tellers arrive early and stand behind a shutter; the branch manager raises the shutter once (count down from 1 to 0) and all ten tellers start serving customers at the same moment. The completion gate is the reverse: the end-of-day supervisor waits at the door while ten tellers each close their till and report done; only when all ten have reported (count from 10 down to 0) does the supervisor lock up. The shutter is single-use — once raised it stays raised. If you need a shutter that goes up and down every day, you use a CyclicBarrier instead.
s1_definition.oneliner: CountDownLatch is a one-time gate — count 1 to release many waiters at once (startup), or count N to let one coordinator wait for all workers (completion); it never resets, so use CyclicBarrier or Phaser for repeated rounds.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `CountDownLatch` is a one-shot synchronization aid initialized with a count. Threads call `await()` to block until the count reaches zero, and other threads call `countDown()` to decrement it. Once it hits zero it stays zero forever — there is no reset. Two canonical patterns exist: a startup gate (count 1) where many worker threads wait on a single latch so they all begin at the same instant, and a completion gate (count N) where a coordinator waits for N workers to each count down as they finish. Because a latch cannot be reused, for repeated phases you use `CyclicBarrier` or `Phaser`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The startup gate is like a bank branch where ten tellers arrive early and stand behind a shutter; the branch manager raises the shutter once (count down from 1 to 0) and all ten tellers start serving customers at the same moment. The completion gate is the reverse: the end-of-day supervisor waits at the door while ten tellers each close their till and report done; only when all ten have reported (count from 10 down to 0) does the supervisor lock up. The shutter is single-use — once raised it stays raised. If you need a shutter that goes up and down every day, you use a CyclicBarrier instead.

**One line to remember:** CountDownLatch is a one-time gate — count 1 to release many waiters at once (startup), or count N to let one coordinator wait for all workers (completion); it never resets, so use CyclicBarrier or Phaser for repeated rounds.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India runs an end-of-day settlement where multiple worker threads each settle a slice of trades. For a fair benchmark the operations team wants all workers to start at the exact same instant, not staggered by thread creation time. This is exactly the startup gate: every worker waits on a latch of count 1, and the coordinator counts it down once to release them all simultaneously.

Problem 2 — The report cannot be generated until every settlement worker has finished. The coordinator must wait for all workers. This is the completion gate: a latch of count N where each worker counts down when done and the coordinator awaits zero before producing the summary for SAV2001 and CUR3001.

Problem 3 — If one worker crashes, the coordinator must not hang forever. A timed await raises an alert. And because this runs every single day, a one-shot latch cannot be reused for tomorrow's run, so the code shows why you would switch to a CyclicBarrier for repeated daily rounds.

The code builds a `SettlementWorker` that waits on the start gate, settles its slice, and counts down the done gate, a `SettlementCoordinator` that opens the start gate and awaits completion, and a demo that runs both gates end to end.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: 4 workers, start gate count 1, done gate count 4, SAV2001 starting at Rs.1,000,000, each worker debits Rs.10,000.

Step 1: Four worker tasks are submitted. Each immediately calls `startGate.await()` and blocks, because the start gate count is still 1. They are all parked, none has started real work.

Step 2: The coordinator calls `startGate.countDown()`, dropping the count from 1 to 0. All four workers unblock at the same instant — this is the startup gate releasing many waiters together.

Step 3: Each worker logs that it started, calls `debit(10000)`, and in its finally block calls `doneGate.countDown()`. The done gate count drops 4 to 3 to 2 to 1 to 0 as workers finish. SAV2001 goes 1,000,000 to 990,000 to 980,000 to 970,000 to 960,000.

Step 4: The coordinator, blocked in `doneGate.await(5, SECONDS)`, unblocks when the count reaches 0 and returns true (within the timeout). This is the completion gate — one coordinator waiting for all workers.

Step 5: The coordinator generates the report and logs the final balance Rs.960,000. If one worker had crashed without the finally block, the done gate would never reach zero and the timed await would return false, triggering the alert.

```
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: coordinator: firing the starting gun
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: worker 0 started settling
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: worker 2 started settling
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: worker 1 started settling
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: worker 3 started settling
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: worker 0 done
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: worker 1 done
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: worker 2 done
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: worker 3 done
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: coordinator: all workers finished, generating report
Oct 21, 2026 ... INFO: Report: SAV2001 balance = Rs.960000
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — CountDownLatch Gates ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Latch (one-shot gate): startup + completion             │
  │     WHY: simultaneous start, single coordinator join     │
  │  Note: repeated rounds → CyclicBarrier/Phaser (resettable)│
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: Worker settles, Coordinator orchestrates — 1 job     │
  │  O: more workers = larger done count, code unchanged     │
  │  D: both depend on CountDownLatch abstraction            │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   CountDownLatch (JDK)                 │
  │  - count: int (AQS state)             │
  │  + await(): void                      │  blocks until 0
  │  + await(t, unit): boolean            │  timed
  │  + countDown(): void                  │  decrement, no-op at 0
  └───────────────┬───────────────────────┘
          used by  │
       ┌───────────┴────────────┐
       ▼                        ▼
  ┌──────────────┐        ┌────────────────────┐
  │ Settlement   │        │ SettlementCoordinator│
  │ Worker       │        │ - startGate          │ ◇
  │ - startGate  │        │ - doneGate           │ ◇
  │ - doneGate   │        │ + run()              │
  │ + run()      │        └────────────────────┘
  └──────────────┘

  Contract for await():
    Pre:  none
    Post: returns when count==0 (or timeout → false)
  Contract for countDown():
    Post: count = max(0, count-1); never blocks; put in finally

  State: count N → ... → 0 (terminal, cannot reset)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
CountDownLatch is a one-shot synchronization aid that you create with a count. Threads that call await block until the count reaches zero, and other threads call countDown to decrement it. The key word is one-shot: once the count hits zero it stays zero forever, there is no way to raise it again.

There are two patterns I use it for. The first is a startup gate, where I create a latch with a count of one, every worker calls await at the top of its task, and a coordinator calls countDown exactly once when everything is ready. That single countDown is the starting gun, and all the workers that were waiting unblock at the same instant. This is how you get a fair simultaneous start instead of a staggered one. The second is a completion gate, where I create a latch whose count equals the number of workers, each worker calls countDown in a finally block when it finishes, and a coordinator calls await to block until every worker has reported done. That lets one coordinator wait cleanly for a whole batch to complete before it moves on.

Two practices matter in production. I always put countDown in a finally block, because if a worker crashes before decrementing, the coordinator waits forever. And I use the timed version of await that returns a boolean, so if a worker stalls the coordinator times out, gets back false, and raises an alert instead of hanging the whole end-of-day run.

The limitation drives the follow-up question. Because a latch cannot be reset, it is wrong for anything that repeats. At National Bank of India our settlement runs every single day, so for the per-round rendezvous inside a run I used a CyclicBarrier, which automatically resets itself at the end of each cycle, and where I needed dynamic registration across multiple phases I used a Phaser. The sentence I give interviewers is that CountDownLatch is a single-use gate — count one to release many waiters together for a simultaneous start, or count N to let one coordinator wait for all workers to finish — and the moment I need the gate to open and close repeatedly, I switch to CyclicBarrier or Phaser.

---

keyPoints: Startup gate: workers await, main counts down
Completion gate: main awaits, workers count down
Cannot reset — use CyclicBarrier for reuse
